Non-linear associations of a body shape index with diabetes among adults: A cross-sectional study
Abstract
Objective: This study aimed to explore the relationship between a body shape index (ABSI) and diabetes, and to assess the robustness of this relationship across different population subgroups.
Methods: Utilizing data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) database, this study employed multivariate linear regression analysis to evaluate the association between ABSI and the likelihood of having diabetes. This research further explored non-linear issues in gender stratification through smooth curve fitting and two-part linear regression models, analyzing different subgroups including gender, race, hypertension, and stroke.
Results: A total of 34,693 participants were involved in the study, with a diabetes prevalence of 11.60%. The prevalence increased with higher tertiles of ABSI. After comprehensive adjustment, ABSI was positively correlated with diabetes (OR = 1.42, 95% CI: 1.33, 1.52). Participants in the highest quartile of ABSI had a 96% higher odds of having diabetes (OR = 1.96, 95% CI: 1.69, 2.26), than did those in the lowest quartile. Smooth curve fitting analysis revealed a non-linear, inverse L-shaped relationship between ABSI and diabetes, with a breakpoint at 9.54. Subgroup analyses indicated that the association between ABSI and diabetes remained stable across different populations, except for those with a history of stroke.

input.line_text: This finding contrasts sharply with a previous study that did not detect a threshold effect between ABSI and diabetes [30]. In that cohort, the association remained consistently positive—and essentially linear—across the entire observed range of ABSI, with no apparent non-linear pattern even after multivariable adjustment [30]. Several factors may explain this discrepancy, most notably differences in the racial and regional composition of the two study populations. Our sample was drawn from NHANES and is therefore representative of the U.S. population, whereas the earlier study was conducted in a Japanese cohort [30]. Such differences in race and geography may plausibly account for the divergent patterns observed [44–49]. In particular, Asian and non-Asian populations differ substantially in body fat distribution, insulin sensitivity, and diabetes-related genetic variants, all of which may influence the sensitivity and specificity of ABSI in predicting diabetes risk [44–46]. Beyond these biological differences, lifestyle and environmental factors—including dietary habits, physical activity levels, and socioeconomic status—also vary markedly across regions and are known to shape diabetes risk [47–49]. Collectively, these considerations suggest that the non-linear pattern identified here may be specific to this population rather than a universal feature of the ABSI–diabetes relationship, underscoring the value of validating population-specific ABSI thresholds in future studies.

input.text_to_find: In this study, we observed a significant positive

input.line_text: In this study, we observed a significant positive correlation between ABSI and diabetes (Fig 2 and Table 2). Each unit increase in ABSI was associated with 42% to 66% higher odds of diabetes across multiply adjusted models, and participants in the highest ABSI quartile had nearly 96% higher odds than those in the lowest quartile, supporting ABSI as an independent marker of diabetes risk. These findings are corroborated by previous studies. In the Qatari population, ABSI predicted diabetes risk more strongly than BMI; Bawadi et al. (2019) reported an adjusted odds ratio of 1.85 (95% CI: 1.54–2.23) per 1-SD increment in ABSI versus 1.34 (95% CI: 1.18–1.51) for BMI among 2,536 adults [28]. A rural Chinese study also found a significant association, although ABSI showed lower predictive accuracy than WHtR and BRI (AUC 0.61 in both sexes) [29]. In two Japanese adult cohorts, multivariable Cox regression likewise identified an association with Type 2 diabetes, with consistent results across population subgroups [30, 31]. Despite differences in study design, population, and statistical approach, the evidence collectively supports ABSI as a relevant and broadly applicable marker of diabetes risk.

input.find_text: In this study, we observed a significant positive correlation between ABSI and diabetes, as  in Fig 2 and Table 2. Specifically, our results indicate that each unit increase in ABSI is associated with 42% to 66% higher odds of having diabetes, a finding consistently supported across various models adjusted for multiple variables. Moreover, when ABSI was categorized into quartiles, the highest quartile group were nearly 96% more likely to have diabetes compared to the lowest quartile group. It is worth noting that a rural Chinese study also identified a significant association between ABSI and diabetes risk, although ABSI demonstrated relatively lower predictive accuracy compared to other anthropometric indices such as WHtR and BRI, with an AUC of 0.61 in both men and women [29]. In contrast, our study found a stronger association, with individuals in the highest ABSI quartile having a 96% higher odds of diabetes compared to those in the lowest quartile. While we did not perform a direct comparative analysis between ABSI and other indices in our cohort, the findings collectively suggest that ABSI is a relevant marker for diabetes risk in diverse populations.
